The test image shows soybean plants at soil level with severe stem/root damage. I can see:
- Very dark, blackened/rotted stem tissue at the soil line
- Dead/dying plants with dried pods
- Dark discoloration concentrated at the base of stems
- Some orange-brown tissue visible

Top candidates: Phytophthora (dark chocolate-brown stem from soil line), White_Mold (black sclerotia on stems), Charcoal_Rot (gray with black specks), Rhizoctonia. Let me view reference images.

Now I have 21 reference images viewed. Let me analyze the evidence:

**Test image key features:**
- Low-angle view at soil/crown level of mature soybean plants
- Very dark, nearly black tissue concentrated at stem bases at the soil line
- Some orange-brown coloration within the dark area
- Dead/dried plants with pods still attached
- Multiple plants killed in the area
- Some healthy green plants visible in the background

**Candidate comparison:**

- **Phytophthora**: Reference shows dark chocolate-brown stem discoloration from soil upward, dead plants with leaves staying attached — matches the severe darkening at the base and overall plant death pattern. The Phytophthora reference top-left panel shows a nearly identical field-level picture of dead plants with dark crown/base.
- **Rhizoctonia**: Shows reddish-brown lesions at soil line but more localized/less severe than what I see.
- **Charcoal_Rot**: Gray stem with charcoal-dust specks — the test image is darker/more rotted-looking, not the streaked-gray pattern characteristic of charcoal rot.
- **Sudden_death_syndrome**: Shows white pith (distinct from brown stem rot) and interveinal leaf chlorosis — I don't see the foliar symptom pattern here.
- **Fusarium**: Extremely black, rotted root mass — possible, but Fusarium typically shows more fibrous root destruction without the concentrated crown darkening.

The severely darkened, brown-to-black stem tissue concentrated at the soil line with mature plants killed (leaves/pods still attached to dead stems) is most consistent with **Phytophthora** root and stem rot.
